I mostly just leave it and forget it. Lots of drip irrigation, chop and drop, and casting seed. Excluding actually starting and transplanting everything, its relatively maintenance free if you don't mind the occasional weed or insect damage. My wife says I spend more time walking around and looking at things than I do actually working on it.

If I hadn't planned it well enough, it would probably be a lot more work. My irrigation is set on large zones, subdivided into smaller polyculture guilds each with valves I can adjust to the water needs. Took some time last year trying to get everything adjusted, but now I just turn on a valve to the main zone and let it do its thing.

There is a permaculture group that wanted to come help me last year with planting, but I turned them down because I was still planning while I was planting and didn't want them waiting on me. May take them up on it this spring because I need to get started on turning the basement into livable space for the kids.

Its mostly about planning through all stages of growth. You aren't going to get a huge amount of your typical garden veggies like tomatoes or broccoli crammed in there, but you can get a variety of other things that don't need as much space. I'll give you an example with a bed I have that's roughly a triangle, the short side being about 10 foot, the long being about 30 foot. The first things to come up are garlics, shallots, crocuses, and radishes. Behind them petunias and pansies start spreading out to take over the blooming once the crocuses die back. Towards the larger end of the triangle is a raised rock garden, and the lavender, rosemary, sage, thymes, soapwort, a few primroses and edelweiss start doing their thing. Those kinda form a ring around the raised portion, and I sow poppies in the opening in the middle. Around the base of the rocks, which gives me about a foot and a half between the rocks and the path, I plant leeks, endives, escarole, some lettuces that require more attention than normal, perennial sorrel, some ulmaria like plant to bring in wasps(this year its filipendula/meadowsweet), and generally whatever is handy to fill in the gaps in between. Moving towards the little end of the triangle from the rock garden, I've got three elderberries on the north side, fronted by several large bergamot plants, themselves fronted by large reseeding annual phlox. There's different types of basil scattered through it, and I usually scatter carrot seed over this whole area. Come fall when I cut the plants back, I can harvest the carrots. They don't need a lot of sun. Also have a little patch of munchenerbier radishes, as I will probably only use those two or three times a year. There's also an apricot tree between the elderberries and rock garden, but its only about 3 foot high right now. When it gets larger I will pollard it and any shade it casts will be on the house rather than the plants around it. Behind the elderberries and apricot are caraway, spinach, and rutabaga. The rutabaga doesnt get all the light it needs during the summer, but they are hardy enough that once fall hits and the elderberries drop their leaves, it can finish up despite frosts or dustings of snow. Further down towards the tip of the triangle are two honey berry bushes. They aren't super huge right now, but big enough to produce a few berries and take large numbers of cuttings from. Around them are lots of czech radishes which reseed quickly, so I'll get two or three full crop cycles out of them over a growing season by leaving a dozen to go to seed. There's also a columbine, and another variety of pansies, and probably more stuff I've forgotten about. The strawberries from the other side of the path have crossed over and started to spread into the area as well, and I'll let them. They make a pretty good living mulch and the taller plants keep them from being too invasive.

Think of it being the shorter bushier plants growing on the south side, with medium height plants through the middle, then less bushy but taller plants on the north side, with plants that bolt quickly shaded and protected in the dappled shade behind them.
